scenes.narration: The rise of Shimon Peres was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. He was a member of twelve cabinets and represented five political parties in a political career spanning 70 years. Peres was elected to the Knesset in November 1959 and except for three months out of office in early 2006, served as a member of the Knesset continuously until he was elected president in 2007.

Setbacks came early for Shimon Peres, and the response to them is the real story. Serving in the Knesset for 48 years (with the first uninterrupted stretch lasting more than 46 years), Peres is the longest serving member in the Knesset's history. From a young age, he was renowned for his oratorical brilliance, and was chosen as a protégé by David Ben-Gurion, Israel's founding father.

The legacy of Shimon Peres outlived the circumstances that produced it. He began his political career in the late 1940s, holding several diplomatic and military positions during and directly after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War. His first high-level government position was as deputy director general of defense in 1952 which he attained at the age of 28, and director general from 1953 until 1959.

Few lives travel as far as that of Shimon Peres, and the distance is the point. In 1956, he took part in the historic negotiations on the Protocol of Sèvres, which was described by British prime minister Anthony Eden as the "highest form of statesmanship". Kennedy, which resulted in the sale of Hawk anti-aircraft missiles to Israel, the first sale of U.S. military equipment to Israel.

The childhood of Shimon Peres contains the adult in small print. Peres represented Mapai, Rafi, the Alignment, Labor and Kadima in the Knesset, and led Alignment and Labor. Peres first succeeded Yitzhak Rabin as acting prime minister briefly during 1977, before becoming prime minister from 1984 to 1986.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Shimon Peres — in that order. As foreign minister under Prime Minister Rabin, Peres engineered the 1994 Israel–Jordan peace treaty, and won the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize together with Rabin and Yasser Arafat for the Oslo Accords peace talks with the Palestinian leadership. Shimon Peres was born Szymon Perski, on 2 August 1923, in Wiszniew, Poland (now Vishnyeva, Belarus), to Yitzhak (1896–1982) and Sara (1903–1969, née Meltzer) Perski.

The turning point in the life of Shimon Peres looked like a failure at the time. The family spoke Hebrew, Yiddish and Russian at home, and Peres learned Polish at school. His father was a wealthy timber merchant, later branching out into other commodities; his mother was a librarian.

Every biography of Shimon Peres has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Lauren Bacall called me, said that she wanted to meet, and we did. We sat and talked about where our families came from, and discovered that we were from the same family ... but I'm not exactly sure what our relation is ...

The education of Shimon Peres happened mostly outside any school. Peres told Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson that he had been born as a result of a blessing his parents had received from a chassidic rebbe and that he was proud of it. Peres's grandfather, Rabbi Zvi Meltzer, a grandson of Rabbi Chaim Volozhin, had a great impact on his life.

What Shimon Peres wanted at the start and what Shimon Peres got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. In 1932, Peres's father immigrated to Mandatory Palestine and settled in Tel Aviv. He attended Balfour Elementary School and High School, and Geula Gymnasium (High School for Commerce) in Tel Aviv.

The defining trait of Shimon Peres was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. At 15, he transferred to Ben Shemen agricultural school and lived on Kibbutz Geva for several years. During World War II, Peres' father enlisted in the British Army as a sapper in the Royal Engineers and was captured in Greece, returning to Palestine after spending most of the war as a POW.

Those who met Shimon Peres at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. During his captivity, he hid his Jewish identity and was an inmate at Camp E715, a subcamp for POWs that was part of the Auschwitz concentration camp complex. While imprisoned there he met Charles Coward and may have helped him save Jewish Auschwitz inmates.

The private years of Shimon Peres explain the public decades better than any speech. After a failed escape attempt he was saved from execution by an Australian military chaplain. Peres' mother worked in a military parts factory and his future wife also served in the British Army as a nurse and truck driver.

The family Shimon Peres came from matters more than the legends admit. Peres by contrast showed more interest in local pioneering than the war effort, stating at the time that "the army and the war don't interest me." In 1941, he was elected Secretary of HaNoar HaOved VeHaLomed, a Labor Zionist youth movement. He was one of the founding pioneers of kibbutz Alumot, and did agricultural work while writing book reviews and newspaper opinion pieces.

The first real success of Shimon Peres arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. At age 20, he was elected to the HaNoar HaOved VeHaLomed national secretariat, where he was only one of two Mapai party supporters, out of the 12 members. Three years later, he took over the movement and won a majority.

The last chapter of Shimon Peres was written long after the fame. The head of Mapai, David Ben-Gurion, and Berl Katznelson began to take an interest in him, and appointed him to Mapai's secretariat. In 1944, Peres led an illicit expedition into the Negev, then a closed military zone requiring a permit to enter.

The whole life of Shimon Peres reads like a single decision repeated. The group was arrested by a Bedouin camel patrol led by a British officer, taken to Beersheba (then a small Arab town) and incarcerated in the local jail. All of the participants were sentenced to two weeks in prison, and as the leader, Peres was also heavily fined.

Between the birth and the legend of Shimon Peres lie the years that actually decide it. The expedition came across a nest of bearded vultures, called peres in Hebrew, and from this Peres took his Hebrew name. All of Peres's relatives who remained in Wiszniew in 1941 were murdered during the Holocaust, many of them (including Rabbi Meltzer) burned alive in the town's synagogue.

The reputation of Shimon Peres was built in the middle, not at the edges. In 1946, Peres and Moshe Dayan were chosen as the two youth delegates in the Mapai delegation to the Zionist Congress in Basel. In 1947, Peres joined the Haganah, the predecessor of the Israel Defense Forces.

Somebody like Shimon Peres should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. David Ben-Gurion made him responsible for personnel and arms purchases; he was appointed to head the naval service when Israel received independence in 1948. Peres was director of the Defense Ministry's delegation in the United States in the early 1950s.

The life of Shimon Peres begins far from where the story usually starts. While in the U.S. he studied English, economics, and philosophy at The New School and New York University, and completed a four-month advanced management course at Harvard University. In 1952, Peres was appointed deputy director general of the Ministry of Defense, and the following year, he was promoted to director general.

Shimon Peres was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. At age 29, he was the youngest person to hold this position. He was involved in arms purchases and establishing strategic alliances that were important for the State of Israel.

To understand where Shimon Peres ended up, start with where Shimon Peres began. He was instrumental in establishing close relations with France, securing massive amounts of quality arms that, in turn, helped to tip the balance of power in the region. Owing to Peres's mediation, Israel acquired the advanced Dassault Mirage III French jet fighter, established the Dimona nuclear reactor and entered into a tri-national agreement with France and the United Kingdom, positioning Israel in what would become the 1956 Suez Crisis.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Shimon Peres ran through years nobody filmed. Peres continued as a primary intermediary in the close French-Israeli alliance from the mid-1950s, although from 1958, he was often involved in tense negotiations with Charles de Gaulle over the Dimona project. From 1954, as director general of the Ministry of Defense, Peres was involved in the planning of the 1956 Suez War, in partnership with France and Britain.

Each stage of the life of Shimon Peres made the next stage possible. Peres was sent by David Ben-Gurion to Paris, where he held secret meetings with the French government. Peres was instrumental in negotiating the Franco-Israeli agreement for a military offensive.

The people who knew Shimon Peres young describe someone already restless. In November 1954, Peres visited Paris, where he was received by the French defense minister Marie-Pierre Kœnig, who told him that France would sell Israel any weapons it wanted to buy. By early 1955, France was shipping large amounts of weapons to Israel.

What Shimon Peres built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. In April 1956, following another visit to Paris by Peres, France agreed to disregard the Tripartite Declaration, and supply more weapons to Israel. During the same visit, Peres informed the French that Israel had decided upon war with Egypt in 1956.

By the time Shimon Peres reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Throughout the 1950s, an extraordinarily close relationship existed between France and Israel, characterised by unprecedented cooperation in the fields of defense and diplomacy. For his work as the architect of this relationship, Peres was awarded the highest order of the French, the Legion of Honor, as Commander.
